inscription_identified: RIB 1065 — Bilingual Latin-Palmyrene tombstone of Regina and Barates, South Shields (Arbeia Roman Fort), 2nd century AD
published_reading: RGYNᵓ BT ḤRY BR ᶜTᵓ ḤBL
corrected_translation: Regina, the freedwoman of Barates, alas
verbatim_source: RIB 1065 (Roman Inscriptions of Britain); confirmed by Wikipedia article on Tombstone of Regina and multiple museum collections (British Museum, Arbeia/North East Museums). The Palmyrene line is a common funerary formula expressing grief at death. BT = daughter (bt/brt in Aramaic), BR = son (in Aramaic), but in this context BT ḤRY BR ᶜTᵓ does NOT mean 'daughter of Ḥary, son of ʿAttā' (a genealogical reading). Instead, the entire phrase means 'freedwoman of Barates' — a status descriptor, not a paternal genealogy. ḤRY and ᶜTᵓ are NOT personal names here but part of the descriptor 'freedwoman' (from the root meaning 'to be free'). The formula follows standard Palmyrene funerary convention: name + status + lament (ḤBL = alas).
citation: Roman Inscriptions of Britain (RIB 1065); Tombstone of Regina (Wikipedia); Warwick University—Regina of Arbeia; Aramaic Inscriptions in the Palmyra Museum (Syria journal); Hillers & Cussini, Palmyrene Aramaic Texts (Comprehensive Aramaic Lexicon Project)
notes: The proposed reading treated HRY and ćTᵓ as personal names within a genealogical formula ('daughter of Ḥari, son of ʿAttā'), consistent with standard Palmyrene naming practice (e.g., 'Aqma, daughter of Ḥairan'). However, all authoritative sources unanimously translate the Palmyrene line as 'freedwoman of Barates' — a status marker, not paternal descent. The etymology of 'freedwoman' in Aramaic may derive from a root cognate with the elements mistaken for names, but the lexical consensus is unambiguous: this is a freedwoman's epitaph, not a genealogical record. Barates, a Palmyrene merchant, erected this bilingual monument (Latin + Palmyrene) in honor of his wife Regina (a Catuvellaunian Briton, aged 30) in the late 2nd century at South Shields.
